California Taxes: Where the Money Comes From and Where It Goes

Historical California tax revenue and spending, state and local. Every chart is built from public data fetched by the scripts in scripts/; see the repository for sources and methods. Dollar amounts are by fiscal year (ending June 30). Use the buttons above each chart to switch between nominal dollars, inflation-adjusted dollars, per-person, and share-of-total views.

State government

State Data Overview

California's state government collects revenue into the General Fund (flexible, mostly income and sales tax) and special funds (earmarked, e.g. gas taxes for roads). Spending also includes bond funds and federal funds.

Sources (all fetched by scripts/fetch_*.py, listed with hashes in data/raw/MANIFEST.csv):

  • Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) historical revenues, 1950-51 to present, and historical expenditures, 1984-85 to present. These come from Department of Finance and State Controller data.
  • State Controller's Office (SCO) Cities, Counties and Special Districts annual reports (revenues and expenditures, FY2002-03 on), via the SCO's open-data API.
  • BLS CPI-U (via FRED) for inflation, and FRED/Census California population. Census files for county FIPS codes and boundaries.

Caveats

  • The revenue series has a break between 2015-16 and 2016-17: LAO publishes the two periods under different accounting categories, so levels shift slightly. Charts mark the break.
  • 2018-19 personal income and sales tax figures in LAO's file are misaligned; those cells are replaced with DOF Schedule 3 totals (all funds). Every comparison and repair is logged in data/processed/revenue_reconciliation.csv.
  • Local data (SCO) ends at FY2023-24 and excludes K-12 school districts and community colleges, which report to the Department of Education. K-12 districts are covered separately from Census data (FY1992-2024); community colleges are not covered.
  • The newest years (shaded "estimate") are budget estimates and proposals, not closed books.
  • Real dollars use CPI-U (US city average) and the latest complete fiscal year as the base.

Local government

Local Government Revenue

Cities, counties and special districts report finances to the State Controller's Office (SCO). Fiscal years 2002-03 on.

Read this first

  • Not included: K-12 school districts and community colleges report to the Department of Education, not the SCO, so they are not here. Most property tax ultimately funds schools, so these charts understate total local tax collection. County and city tax charts below show what cities and counties themselves receive. K-12 districts have their own page (Census data) in the next section; community colleges are not covered anywhere on this site yet.
  • Double counting: counties receive large state and federal aid ("intergovernmental"), which also shows up in state spending. Do not add state and local totals without netting this out.
  • Reporting break: SCO changed its category format in FY2016-17, so some groups shift at the dotted line. Internal service funds and fund-type categories (special districts) only exist after the change.
  • Values are as reported by each government (SCO does not audit them), in nominal dollars unless the toggle says otherwise.

Local Taxes

Taxes collected by cities and counties, by type. SCO classifies franchise fees under taxes; they're shown separately here. 'Property tax in lieu of VLF' replaced the vehicle license fee revenue the state cut in 2004.

State and local taxes together

State taxes (all funds) next to city and county taxes. Excludes school districts (see the school page) and special districts, so local taxes are understated.

Property tax by recipient

Property tax collected by each kind of local government, 2003 on. The school-district series is from the Census (see the school page); city and county are SCO. Special districts (fire, water, parks) and community colleges also get property tax but are not separable in the data used here, so the total is understated. 'Property tax in lieu of VLF' is excluded.

Local Government Spending

By function. Cities and counties report spending in functional groups that SCO redefined in FY2016-17; this page maps both eras onto one set of groups using the finest reported label (see src/ca_taxes/local.py). City utilities, sanitation and transportation moved between categories at the break, so treat jumps at the dotted line as reporting, not policy.

Special districts

Water, power, hospital, fire, transit and other special districts, by activity (top 12 by cumulative spending).

K-12 School Districts

California's roughly 1,000 school districts spend about half as much as all cities and counties combined. They report to the Department of Education and the Census Bureau rather than the State Controller, so they come from a separate source: the Census Annual Survey of School System Finances, fiscal years 1992-2024 (FY2024 = school year 2023-24).

Read this first

  • State aid dominates and is not new money: roughly half of district revenue is state aid (mostly Proposition 98), which is already counted in state spending. Do not add it to state totals; the burden page uses only the districts' own local taxes.
  • Local property tax: the "Local property tax" layer is what districts collect directly. Part of it exists because the state shifted property tax from cities, counties and special districts to schools in 1992-93 (ERAF) and later years, so the local mix reflects state decisions.
  • Break at FY2019: Census reclassified over 900 California charter schools (those whose charters are held by non-governmental entities) out of the school systems it surveys, so district revenue, spending and enrollment all step down that year. Marked with a dotted line. Per-pupil lines also jump there: enrollment falls by more than spending, and Census notes the state raised its contributions to school employee pensions that year.
  • FY1994 is missing: the Census file for that year covers only 258 of about 1,080 districts, so it is left out and lines cross the gap.
  • Not included: community colleges (also Proposition 98) are not in this survey. County offices of education are included as districts.
  • Totals follow Census' published state tables: transfers between school systems are excluded from both revenue and spending. Fiscal year ends June 30; the survey's FY2024 is the school year ending in 2024.

Per pupil

Spending and revenue per enrolled student, in constant dollars (fall enrollment as reported in the survey). Enrollment peaked around 2005 and was roughly flat to 2018; the drop in FY2019 is mostly the charter-school reclassification, not lost students.

County Maps: Local Taxes and Spending per Person

For each county: taxes collected by the county government plus every city in it, divided by the county's population. San Francisco (a combined city-county) is reported as a city by the SCO and added from there. Excludes school and special districts. Latest year available, nominal dollars.

Putting it together

Total Taxes per Person

State taxes plus city, county and K-12 school district taxes, per Californian. This counts taxes California governments *collect*, not what households pay (federal taxes are excluded, and some state tax is paid by businesses and visitors).

Left out: special districts and community colleges. School districts here means local property and other local taxes only; the state aid they receive (about half of school revenue) is already counted in state spending.

As a share of personal income

Taxes collected divided by total personal income of California residents (BEA, via FRED; fiscal-year average of quarterly rates). This is a rough yardstick of how big government's take is relative to the economy, not an average household tax rate: businesses, visitors and non-residents also pay California taxes, and income here excludes corporate profits retained by firms.

Explore

City and County Explorer

Pick any of California's 482 cities or 57 counties and see taxes and spending per resident over time, then compare cities side by side. Fiscal years 2003-2024, from the State Controller's Office (SCO), in constant dollars.

How to read it

  • Taxes are what the city or county itself levies (property, sales, hotel, utility users, business license, franchise and other taxes). Spending is everything it spends, including enterprise services such as water, power, airports and hospitals, which many cities run and others leave to special districts. High spending per person often reflects those services, not higher taxes or waste.
  • Per person uses the population the government reports to the SCO. San Francisco is both a city and a county and appears here as a city. Population is the SCO's own estimate, not the Census count; two cities' populations are swapped in some SCO years (Mt. Shasta and Mountain View) and are corrected here (population_repaired in data/processed/local_entities.csv).
  • Incomplete picture: residents also pay county, school, special-district and state taxes not shown for a city. Counties spend on behalf of everyone in them, including cities' residents.
  • The SCO changed its reporting format in FY2016-17, so spending (but much less so taxes) can shift at that year.

Highest and lowest taxes per person

Cities with at least 25,000 residents, latest year (nominal dollars). The top is tourist and commercial centers (Beverly Hills, Palm Springs, Santa Monica, Monterey) and Bay Area cities, plus San Francisco, which is a combined city-county; part of the gap is visitors, workers and shoppers who pay tax but are not counted as residents. The bottom is mostly inland suburbs and lower-income cities in the Inland Empire and Central Valley.
